articles.title: HackerTube: YouTube built from videos recommended by HN
articles.summary: YouTube-style UI over 6,454 videos sourced from 39,834 HN comments since 2007.https://hackertube.org/

top_comments: I think there is a massive opportunity for this kind of feed disaggregation. Used to be the recommender and indexing of content was hard, now I believe we can likely build our own according to our own preferences.Haiku/Sonnet (or even Jev) can do a lot of the filtering work to rank and extend an RSS feed list.I think this gives us an opportunity to fully cut the cord from eyeball merchants who want us to maximally engage and therefore polarize their content.The big remaining hook will be the social graph; I am interested to see how far the EU push for mandatory interoperability will go. Another angle I’d support would be mandatory pluggable standards for your own ranking algorithm, but it captures less of the win than full disaggregation.
Made a books version of this: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50326821PS: thank you karpathy, been binging videos on hackertube.org

I often wonder if AI generated programming is ethically positive, whereas AI generated media is problematic.I don't have the answer yet, but it is fairly clear that the lowered barrier to making software is helping to untangle us from software monopolies, as people keep spinning up alternatives super quickly!

articles.title: Show HN: HackerBooks – HackerTube, but for books mentioned on HN
articles.summary: Saw Karpathy's HackerTube and wanted the same thing for books. So I had Claude build one (Opus 5.5).It's ~16.5k books that at least two different HN commenters brought up, from 2007 till now. Each book links back to the comments that mentioned it. Data is downloadable from the about page.To be clear: Claude wrote almost all of it, including the data pipeline and the site. I mostly steered and made calls, bought the domain name, etc.It counts mentions, so it's not perfect (praising a book and trashing it both count). If your favourite book is missing or matched to the wrong thing, tell me.

top_comments: "Top All Time" -> 3rd row -> "Mein Kampf"Sweet.
Fun skimming through this. I wondered how it would deal with book nicknames and chuckled when I found this entry https://hackerbooks.org/#/book/OL15190817W

articles.title: The AI cost of JavaScript frameworks
articles.summary: The AI cost of JavaScript frameworks

top_comments: The are some very real costs to JavaScript frameworks. These frameworks do not exist to empower developers. They exist to:* so that employers do not have to invest in training developers.* to ease candidate selection at hiring, which greases the wheels of hiring/firingIn the big corporate world, especially at non-software companies, there is a culture that strongly believes internally written software sucks. This is Invented Here syndrome, and it reflects that internal developers cannot write software and employers will not invest in maintenance.The larger costs there are human costs, the inability to efficiently solve any problem outside the constraints imposed by the framework.

IMO the largest true value of the frameworks (and languages to some extent) is how they help long-running projects with many people coming and going. The most valuable trait was not what framework allowed, but what framework disallowed, preventing foot guns. E.g. Java got popular because it forced everyone to code similarly, at least more similar than other languages at that time.But for agents it doesn't matter, so why frameworks at all?PS: authors comparison is not relevant, as it's simple mostly-static app with very little cross-dependencies, localizations, component re-usage.

> Frontends are rewritten because some framework or another is “better for agents.” (Did anyone think to ask the agents?) The resulting code is “faster,” the agents make “fewer mistakes,” etc.Yes, of course they asked.The agents responded with how this framework is X, not Y. How creating it was a sharp commentary on other frameworks. A couple honest caveats, and a succinct bottom line that adequately kissed the user's ass.

articles.title: Mathematics has changed. Let's act like it
articles.summary: Mathematics has changed. Let's act like it

top_comments: > To me, someone who chooses a worthwhile problem, obtains a proof completely using AI, understands it thoroughly, and uses it to develop interesting further questions or directions has made a substantial mathematical contribution. I would give that person substantial credit even if they supplied no new ingredient in the original proof.Yup. This is what Terence Tao has been saying about digestion of results for several months now. Mathematics has become a field where results themselves matter less, the social aspect of attracting others to understand your results and explore new problems has become more important.In a sense it is a little bit like software engineering, where writing code can sometimes be delegated to AI, and is arguably less important than understanding what the customer really wants from this software.
Please can we add the name of the guest authors in the titles of these posts?

Isn't it the passage of mathematics from the age of craftsmanship to the age of industrial making ?My recent take on AI is that people haven't adapted to the new huge potential of the tool, and don't dream big enough (yet).It's like seeing a car engine for the first time, lamenting about the future of horses, and not realizing it'll also help us fly.

articles.title: Ask HN: Which TV do you recommend for privacy?
articles.summary: I haven’t owned a TV in years and would like one that respects my privacy. Are there any TV’s which do this well? I am looking for something in the 60”to 80”range and would like a 4k display with at least 60hz display. I don’t mind paying a premium.I have heard good things about Apple TV as a better alternative to most smart TV native apps. Would some TV’s pair better with this than others for privacy? I don’t want the TV doing anything other than being the display for Apple TV.I am curious what success others have had.

top_comments: - Buy an LG OLED TV. They're as gorgeous as they are notorious. I just got a 77" LG C6 and it is crazy good.- Root it [0].- Install Glasshouse [1] and disable all telemetry. YOU now own the glass. Now you can chromecast to the TV, use Adfree YouTube, access IP TV, etc etc etc. No point crippling your TV by pulling the wireless module and voiding your warranty.- Install a bunch of cool apps to your TV [2] (there are many more out there besides those listed here)- Restore to Factory Defaults if you ever want / need to unroot and get back to stock e.g. a warranty claimThe only issue is that LG recently closed the vulnerability that made rooting possible so you don't want any firmware released after 2026-10-10 like 43.21.84. Hopefully a new exploit is found that makes rooting possible once again.BTW, you might have heard of Dev Mode on these TVs but they don't allow anywhere near the functionality that rooting provides.[0] https://tv.slada.sk/guides/rooting-guide[1] https://github.com/rorygallagher2024/glasshouse[2] https://www.webosbrew.org/

Recently I've had to deal with this same problem - get a new TV for living room. Personally, I do not watch TV at all, but kids want to see cartoons when having their breakfast. I spent a week reading forums and came to conclusion that best solution would be to buy a "dumb TV" and connect it to a PC I trust, but it appears there are no dump TVs in my rage of 55" and larger. So, I bought "Google TV" based TCL.When I brought it home, I never connected it to Ethernet or WiFi. Instead, I connected it to my laptop over USB, then using adb I uninstalled almost every application from it. It took me quite some time to figure out what app is possible to remove and what should be kept to let TV functionality to work. I even had to factory-default it a couple of times because some random apps I removed were crucial for Android to work. :) I think it took me 5-6 hours to clean it. Now it has only basic TV functionality like any dump TV does, I can watch air and cable TV channels, watch movies and play music from USB storage. If there's a need to watch something online, I connect it over HDMI to my small mini-PC that runs FreeBSD. I think I'm satisfied with the result. :-)PS: Yesterday I opened the case and disconnected WiFi antenna. Just in case.

First of all, open the TV and disconnect the wireless radio from the main board, on mine (Samsung) it was just unplugging one cable (AI or Google it). I dislike doing stuff like that, but it was easy in my case, maybe you'll be lucky, too.Second, never use the "apps" built into the TV.Next, don't plug Ethernet into the TV. Plug HDMI cables into the TV.Use a box of your choice on the other end of the HDMI cables. This is now the box that you trust. (Roku? Shield? Blu-ray? MacBook? PC? Linux? Playstation? XBox? Whatever you want.)The Smart TV itself is now fine. Choose the devices you plug into it to play content. The TV just shows it.

articles.title: Show HN: OmniDiff – Opensource, super fast, content aware Git difftool, in Rust
articles.summary: I have been researching what the ultimate diff tool would look like, based on actual diffs in open source repositories.OmniDiff can diff: code (25 languages), config, images, PDFs, archives, cursors, fonts...It's fast. It can diff C++ files of tens of thousands of lines in under 100ms, on a 2023 ThinkPad T14s.It's open source. AGPLv3.It's based on real diffs. I looked at the 7400 repositories that are listed in Gentoo packages, sampled 2000 diffs and solved them manually to get a good understanding of what is needed, before putting together the diff pipelines for each content type. Incidentally, this also forms the basis of the CI pipeline, so the robustness of the codebase is quite high.I'm still developing it. It's v0.3.0 at this time. But I have been using it daily as my git difftool for months now, and it works well.AI Disclosure: Yes, I do use AI. No, I do not vibecode.

top_comments: > can diff 99.95% of code changesI’m not sure if I’m understanding this correctly : so for the remaining 0.05% of code changes, this tool would just… miss it? That seems horrible for a diff tool :O

For me the biggest issue is “git rebase” merge conflicts because the surrounding context was modified (especially near beginning/end of functions where the context includes unrelated stuff), or similar in a markdown document.(If commit A adds a line to the end of a bullet list in markdown and commit B does the same, they will conflict even though resolution is trivial for a human)
Is there a way to use it with git without having to change your global git config? I.e. `git diff | omnidiff` or something?You can do this with delta: `git diff | delta --side-by-side`
The mistake is thinking the first S is what people pay for when it is the second S.

I am working toward similar goals but with a different approach. With LLMs, software can become more personal, customized, quirky even. Software will fit the last mile better than ever.The solution is not another SaaS. But desktop apps. Less dependence on a cloud. Of course we need backups. And we need networking. Perhaps peer to peer. Or run a tiny VPS.Businesses, families, communities building their own workflows. The agent is at the core. And an agent that can work with any LLM. Build agents for non-technical people. Stick to a tech stack, offer end to end (from prompt to deploying generated code on VPS) out of the box from the harness.

This seems like it’s trying to reinvent the idea of FOSS. There’s already tons of FOSS alternatives to big tech SaaS and there’s lots of tech coops and other venues for tech activism. Why not support one of those ventures or build a platform to help amplify them?Also odd to advocate for control of tech only to cede the entire project to AI.
